methods to suppress the release of CO2, using photo- or electrocatalysis.[7–10] Particularly, the electrocatalytic reduction can be a promising method for managing the global carbon balance and issues regarding energy generation, as it can convert CO2 to C1 or C2 chemical products as fuel.[11,12] However, this reduction process faces significant challenges due to the chemical inertness of CO2, as there are high thermodynamic and kinetic barriers to obtain a successful electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. Additionally, the CO2-to-CO pathway is usually selected, because CO is the raw material of the Fisher–Tropsch process and other added-value hydrocarbons with wide distribution (C1–C3 products).[13–17]
On the other hand, the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and the stable CO bond of CO2 can optimize the catalytic system through the activity and selectivity during the CO2-to-CO electrocatalytic process.[18–21]
Metal- and nitrogen-coordinated materials dispersed on carbon matrix (M–Nx–C), with a high density of active sites, have attracted increased interests in the field of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2, due to their low cost and high abundance of raw material.[22–28] Nitrogen coordinated metal as catalytic sites that could be designable to fit the especial functionality. As is already known, the Cu–Nx–C sites can have much more interaction with the oxygen of the CO2, which can enhance the enthalpy of the CO2 and inhibit the HER but results in sluggish kinetics of the CO2 + H+ + e− → COOH* process.[29,30] Besides, the Fe–Nx–C materials are often applied in CO2 reduction with low onset potential. Nevertheless, the desorption of *CO into the gas phase can reduce the reactivity, due to the strong binding of CO to the Fe–Nx–C sites in the step of COOH* + H+ + e− → CO* + H2O and CO* → CO+ *.[31–33]
Considering the issues mentioned above, to maximize the potential of single-atom catalysts for multistep catalytic reaction, we design and synthesize biatomic active sites of Cu–Fe–N6–C catalyst by pyrolysis of PcCu–Fe–ZIF-8 under an argon atmosphere at 1000  °C (the detail can be found in the Supporting Information). The configuration and coordination environment of the diatomic catalyst are evidenced by the aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) (AC HAADF-STEM) and X-ray adsorption spectroscopy. The experimental results show
To relieve the green gas emission and involve the carbon neutral cycle, electrochemical reduction of CO2 attracts more and more attention. Herein, a biatomic site catalyst of Cu–Fe coordinated with the nitrogen, which is doped in the carbon matrix (denoted as Cu–Fe–N6–C), is designed. The as-obtained Cu–Fe–N6–C exhibits higher performance than that of Cu–N–C and Fe–N–C, owing to bimetallic sites, proving synergistic functions based on different molecules and their interfaces. Cu–Fe–N6–C shows high selectivity toward CO, with high Faradaic efficiency (98% at −0.7 V), and maintaining 98% of its initial selectivity after 10 h electrolysis. The experimental results and theoretical calculations reveal that the synergistic catalysis of different metallic sites enlarges the adsorption enthalpy of CO2, reducing the activation energy result in generating high selectivity, activity, stability, and low impedance.
Due to climate change and the global warming, CO2 emissions become one of the most urgent issues.[1–3] Accordingly, capturing and converting CO2 to value-added chemical products have gained much attentions recently.[4–6] Among them, the reduction of CO2 is considered as one of the most promising

that the catalyst of Cu–Fe–N6–C has higher performance on the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 than the simple Fe or Cu centers, which is also revealed by the density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The exact control of multiactive sites at the atomic level will reveal a novel path for the rational design of multistep catalysts with high performance, based on nonprecious metals for reproducible carbon cycle technologies.
The synthesis pathway of binary atomic Cu–Fe sites dispersed in the N-doped porous matrix carbon catalysts of Cu–Fe–N6–C can be roughly divided into two steps, as illustrated in Figure  1 (the powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) can be found in Figure S1 in the Supporting Information). First, PcCu–Fe–ZIF-8 was fabricated by mixing PcCu, iron nitrate, zinc nitrate, and 2-Me-imidazole. The mixture was stirred overnight to obtain a blue precipitate, as a result of the bonding of PcCu molecules to Fe, which is coordinated to the organic ligand as nodes, so it is ensured that the Cu and Fe species
are dispersed in the framework homogeneously. Subsequently, the blue precipitates were annealed at 1000  °C under an argon atmosphere, and PcCu–Fe–ZIF-8 is carbonized and transformed into binary atomic Cu–Fe sites, dispersed on the nitrogen-doped carbon matrix without any further acid leaching treatment (denoted as Cu–Fe–N6–C; the details can be found in the Supporting Information).
The PXRD pattern of Cu–Fe–N6–C shows a broad peak of 26°, assigned to the graphitic matrix (Figure S2, Supporting Information). The broad peak elucidates the presence of a disordered graphitic matrix, which allows the isolation of Cu–Fe sites loaded on the N-doped carbon. The other two catalysts of Cu–N–C and Fe–N–C show similar PXRD patterns. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images show a uniform rhombic dodecahedron morphology of PcCu–Fe–ZIF-8 with an average diameter of ≈100  nm (Figure S3, Supporting Information). After the annealing process, the as-obtained Cu–Fe–N6–C

is gained without any structural deterioration (Figure  1a). As shown in Figure  1b,c, there are no metal nanoparticles observed on the carbon matrix. Furthermore, the AC HAADFSTEM images (Figure 1d–f) demonstrate that the small bright dual dots, tagged by red cycles, distributed in the carbon matrix can be assigned to Cu and Fe atoms. Moreover, the elemental distribution of Cu, Fe, N, and C is characterized by energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy analysis (Figure 1f). To verify the surface and composition of Cu–N–C, Fe–N–C, and Cu–Fe– N6–C, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was carried out. The porphyrin-like signal at 399.1 eV has been found, being assigned to the metal–nitrogen coordination (Figure S7a–c, Supporting Information).[34] Furthermore, the porosity of the catalysts is characterized by nitrogen isotherms with the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface areas of 760, 602.8, and 876.2 m2 g−1 (Figure S8, Supporting Information). In view of the considered surface area, the CO2 adsorption isotherms under three different temperatures are carried to estimate the affinity of the catalysts toward CO2. Interestingly, the dual single-atom sites show the biggest CO2 enthalpy than the other catalysts, with 32 kJ mol−1 at room temperature (Figure S7, Supporting Information). The X-ray absorption fine spectrum was conducted to investigate the chemical state and coordination environment of Cu and Fe atoms in the catalysts. Figure 2a shows the X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra of Cu single atom (SA) and Cu–Fe–N6–C at the Cu k-edge, along with Cu foil and CuO as references. The absorption edge of Cu k-edge of two samples was located between Cu foil and CuO, indicating that the Cu in Cu–Fe–N6–C and Cu SA were all in a similar oxidation state between Cu0 and Cu2+. The absorption edge of Cu–Fe–N6–C is shifted 0.3 eV toward lower energy relative to Cu SA, indicating that the valence state of Cu–Fe–N6–C is more positive than Cu SA. The Cu foil and CuO references exhibit two well-resolved peaks at 1.59 and 2.23 Å in the Fourier transformed (FT) k3χ(k) curve in the real space (R-space) (Figure  2b), assigned to the shorter CuO bonds in CuO and CuCu bonds in Cu foil, respectively. The FT spectrum of Cu SA appears at 1.47 Å,

which can be assigned to the CuN coordination. However, compared with the FT spectrum of Cu SA, the real-space spectrum of Cu–Fe–N6–C shows a new peak at 2.24 Å, suggesting that Cu–Fe–N6–C has CuN and CuFe/Cu coordinations, respectively. From its corresponding Fe k-edge XANES spectrum (Figure 2c), the absorption edge of Fe SA and Cu–Fe–N6–C was located between FeO and Fe2O3, which suggests that the electronic state of the Fe species is between Fe2+ and Fe3+.
In addition, the energy absorption threshold value of Cu–Fe–N6–C was much lower than that in the case of Fe SA, which revealed that the valence state of Fe species in Cu–Fe–N6–C was lower than that in Fe SA. Furthermore, more structural information about Fe was obtained by the extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) investigations. Compared to the FT spectrum of Fe SA, the Fe k-edge of the FT spectrum of Cu–Fe–N6–C has also two main peaks at 1.44 and 2.24 Å, which were assigned to Fe–N and Fe–Cu/Fe coordinations, respectively. Compared with Fe k-edge and Cu k-edge of the FT spectrum, it is obvious that they all have two peaks, where the first peak corresponds to the coordination of light elements and the second peak is assigned to the coordination of Fe–Fe, Fe–Cu, and Cu–Fe, respectively. However, FT values of Cu and Fe appear at 2.25 Å simultaneously in the same position, indicating that the only possible coordination is the Fe–Cu. Combined with the results of XPS and XAFS, we can conclude that Cu–Fe–N6–C has Fe–N, Cu–N, and Cu–Fe coordination states.
Considering the difficulties in discriminating the Fe/Cu neighbors by EXAFS fittings, we focused our investigation on the combination of DFT calculations with EXAFS simulations to determine the optimized structures of CuN3–FeN3 catalyst. The fitting results of Cu–Fe–N6–C catalyst can reveal the better structural information of the material. From the fitting results of Table S1 (Supporting Information), the Cu–N and Cu–Fe coordination numbers were 3 and 1.1, respectively. Similarly, for the local environment around Fe, the Fe–N and Fe–Cu coordination numbers were 3.1 and 3.1, respectively. Considering the difficulties in discriminating the Fe–Fe, Cu–Cu, or Fe–Cu neighbors by EXAFS, we resort to EXAFS wavelet transform (WT) analysis, which is powerful for discriminating the backscattering atoms even when they overlap substantially in R-space, providing not only radial distance resolution but also k-space resolution. As shown in Figure  2e,f, the WT contour has maxima at 4.0 and 7.6 Å−1 for Fe SA, Cu SA, CuN3–FeN3, and FeN3–CuN3 confirming the presence of FeN, CuN, and FeCu/Cu–Fe bonding. Meanwhile, no maximum intensities corresponding to Fe–Fe and Cu–Cu were observed, comparing with the WT contour plots of Cu foil, CuO, Fe foil, FeO, and Fe2O3 (Figures S9 and S10, Supporting Information). The calculated XANES spectra of these configurations are shown for comparison in Figure  2g,h. Hence, the structural model of “CuN3–FeN3” was considered as shown in Figure 2i. It can be affirmed that the “CuN3–FeN3” configuration was reproducible in the experimental spectrum well.
The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is evaluated in a three-electrode system in CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 (pH 6.8) solution. As revealed by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) (Figure 3a), Cu–Fe–N6–C exhibits the highest total current density from −0.7 to −1.0  V (vs RHE), giving current densities of 7.5 mA cm−2 at −0.7 V and 22.4 mA cm−2 at −1.0 V versus reversible
hydrogen electrode (RHE), respectively, significantly exceeding that of the Fe–N–C and Cu–N–C catalysts. In Ar-saturated KHCO3 solution, Cu–Fe–N6–C shows a much smaller current density than that in the CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution, indicating that the high electrochemical performance of Cu–Fe–N6–C was originated from the CO2RR process (Figure  3a, inset). Meanwhile, the low current density of Fe–N–C and Cu–N–C is attributed to their low faradaic efficiency (FE) at high overpotential.[35] The catalytic performances of Fe–N–C, Cu–N–C, and Cu–Fe–N6–C are evaluated and corresponding FECO values in the potential range from −0.5 to −1.0 are calculated. Cu–Fe–N6–C has a higher FECO value (98% at −0.7  V) than Fe–N–C (65% at −0.9 V) and Cu–N–C (21.7% at −0.6 V) (Figure 3b). The higher current densities and FECO indicate the highly enhanced activity of bimetal–nitrogen sites.
Moreover, to uncover the reaction kinetics of different sites in the electrocatalytic process, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and Tafel plots were carried out (Figure  3d,e). As revealed by the Nyquist plots, the charge-transfer resistance (Rct) of Cu–Fe–N6–C (0.97 Ω) is significantly lower than that of Fe–N–C (4.62 Ω) and Cu–N–C (1.12 Ω), implying the faster charge-transfer rate for Cu–Fe–N6–C catalyst. Besides, the current density of Cu–Fe–N6–C (22.4  mA cm−2 at −1.0  V vs RHE) is obviously increased compared with Fe–N–C (20.6 mA cm−2 at −1.0 V vs RHE) and Cu–N–C (15.5 mA cm−2 at −1.0 V vs RHE), which indicates that the combination of Fe and Cu active sites significantly improves the charge in the catalysis process.
Tafel slopes of Cu–Fe–N6–C (244 mV decade−1) are lower than that of Fe–N–C (259 mV decade−1) and Cu–N–C (257 mV decade−1). The lower Tafel slope of Cu–Fe–N6–C indicates that the electrons can be transferred more easily from the Cu–Fe–N6–C surface to the carbon dioxide molecule for reduction reaction and more favorable kinetics of Cu–Fe–N6–C for the generation of CO.[36,37] The combination of Fe and Cu significantly lowered the Tafel slope of Cu–Fe–N6–C, which indicates that the kinetics of this step is greatly enhanced.
Combining the total current density and the corresponding FECO, the CO partial densities have been obtained under different applied potentials. We can see from Figure  3c that Cu–Fe–N6–C achieved a current density of 3.8  mA cm−2 at −0.7  V, which was 1.8 and 2.6 times higher than those of the other two catalysts (Figure  3c). Cu–Fe–N6–C maintains excellent FECO (>85%) in a wide potential range (from −0.6 to −1.0  V) and reaches up to a maximum FECO value of 98% at −0.7  V. Moreover, Fe–Cu–N6–C also exhibits outstanding durability for CO2RR, maintaining 90% of the initial FE for CO production (7 mA cm−2) after 10 h of continuous electrolysis (Figure  3f). To further investigate the selectivity toward CO2RR, the FE tests are carried out. CO is the main gas product monitored by the gas chromatography (GC), and there is no liquid product detected in the 1H NMR spectroscopy (Figure S11, Supporting Information).
DFT calculations were performed for unveiling the origin of high catalytic activity of the Cu–Fe–N6–C catalyst toward electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO at atomic levels. The computational details can be found in the Supporting Information. Figure  4a shows the free energy profiles for the formation of CO from CO2 on three catalysts, of which

atomic structures are displayed in Figure  4b. Since the solvation effect was reported to be vital in CO2 reduction that can stabilize the bent OCO backbond, we constructed an aqueous environment with some explicit water molecules for investigations.[38] We found that Cu–Fe–N6–C could both i) facilitate the CO2 adsorption and ii) reduce the CO bond breaking barrier. CO2 adsorption energy on Cu–Fe–N6–C was calculated to be −0.03 eV with the C and O atoms both binding to the Fe site (Figure  4c), which is stronger than 0.43 eV on Fe–N–C and 0.61 eV on Cu–N–C (Table S2, Supporting Information). Previous works have shown that the CO bond breaking in COOH* can be catalyzed by the single-metal site or dual-metal sites.[39] On single-metal site catalyst, i.e., Fe–N–C and Cu–N–C, the CO bond breaks in COOH*, where only CO* can adsorb on the metal site and water can accept the dissociated OH group (Figure  4c) that is stabilized by hydrogen bonding. For the Cu–Fe–N6–-C, COOH* breaks the CO bond forming CO* on the Fe site and OH* on the adjacent Cu site. Such a dual-metal site could remarkably reduce the CO bond breaking barrier from 1.24  eV on Fe–N–C and 0.77  eV on the Cu–N–C, to 0.44 eV on Cu–Fe–N6–C. In this work, the dual metal of Cu–Fe sites coordinated with nitrogen dispersed in porous carbon were designed and synthesized to enhance the adsorption enthalpy of CO2, which increases the CO2 concentration during the electrocatalysis process. Combining the experimental results and theoretical calculations, the superb CO2RR performances of Cu–Fe–N6–C are mostly attributed to the bifunctional active sites, because the Cu sites enhanced the concentration of CO2 due to the large affinity between Cu and CO2 while the Fe sites suppressed the hydrogen evolution. This work provides a useful strategy to design target-oriented catalysts for boosting the electrocatalytic reactions using the polynary, synergetic metal sites as well as in-depth understanding of the synergistic effect of the different active sites.
